blurb.en: Say hello the local way, greet elders first, and close a talk politely.
Keep any conversation alive when you don't understand yet.
Answer the first questions everyone asks: name, home, work, family.
Ask prices, bargain fairly, count, pay and get change.
Agree a fare, give directions to a driver and get off where you want.
Get help fast, and handle the pharmacy and the doctor.
Order, say how you like it, and be a good guest at someone's table.
Visit a family home, honour the elders, and leave well.
Make a plan on the phone: when, where, and 'I'll call you back'.
Say how you are, talk about the day, and react like a friend.

am.note: Everyday hello for anyone. To an elder, ጤና ይስጥልኝ (t'ena yəst'əlləñ) is warmer; see st-0041.

en.text: I'm fine, thank you. And you?

am.note: Only 'and you' changes, with the listener. 'I'm fine' is the same for a woman or a man. Many people add እግዚአብሔር ይመስገን (thank God).
Literally 'it has not gone into me'. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'please, repeat it'.
Literally 'please, speak slowly'.
Spoken -ኩ ending (written style: እየተማርሁ).

en.text: How do you say this in Amharic?

am.note: Literally 'what is this called in Amharic?'. Point at the thing.
To get attention, ይቅርታ works for anyone. Amharic: the same words for everyone.
Adapted: Amharic accepts an offer with 'okay, thank you', so there is one form. አዎ፣ እባክህ (f እባክሽ, respect እባክዎ) is for asking ('yes, please do'), not for accepting.
Literally 'can you [do] English?', the everyday way to ask.
Plain everyday word. In a home, መታጠቢያ ቤት (bathroom) is gentler.
Literally 'please, give me water'.
Plain ይቅርታ does not change with the listener, and 'I'm learning' does not change with the speaker, so there is one form.
The morning greeting asks 'how did you spend the night?'. The short ደህና አደርክ? (did you sleep well?) is also used.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'be well'. Among friends in Addis, ቻው (chaw, from Italian 'ciao') is very common.
The evening greeting asks 'how did you spend the evening?'.
Literally 'spend the night well'.
Adapted: to a group people ask 'are you all well?'. In the afternoon, እንደምን ዋላችሁ? (how was your day, all?) is also heard.
Literally 'I'm glad we got to know each other'. Amharic: the same words for everyone.
Literally 'let's meet later', so it does not change with the listener.
Literally 'let's meet tomorrow'. Amharic: the same words for everyone.
Literally 'spend the evening well'.
Literally 'for you too', the answer to a wish like መልካም ቀን ይሁንልህ. After ደህና እደር, the bare አንተም (f አንቺም, respect እርስዎም) is said. አብረን (together) is also a common reply.
Literally 'it's nothing'.
Plain ይቅርታ is the same for everyone. The fuller 'forgive me' changes with the listener: ይቅርታ አድርግልኝ (m), ይቅርታ አድርጊልኝ (f), ይቅርታ ያድርጉልኝ (respect).
Used among Ethiopian Muslims. Most Addis Christians greet with ሰላም.
The fixed reply to the line above.
Base is to an older man (አባባ, 'father'); the variant is to an older woman (እማማ, 'mother'). ጤና ይስጥልኝ is itself a respect greeting. Say it first, with a small bow.

Adapted: the natural reply thanks God, not the person ('I slept well, God be thanked'). The Amharic morning greeting is a question, so the reply has no separate 'good morning'. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.

en.text: Good morning! How did you sleep?

am.note: Said to the learner: the form follows the learner. Greetings come in rounds like this; answer each one.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'it has gone into me'. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.

en.text: Can you write it for me?

am.note: Literally 'is what I said right?'.
Literally 'please, correct me when I make a mistake'.

en.text: Speak to me in Amharic, please.

am.note: Literally 'I thank you because you were patient with me'.
Literally 'a little is left for you. Repeat it.' A teacher's way to say 'almost'.
Amharic asks 'who is your name?', not 'what'.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'it's for work that I came'.
ጠየቀ here means 'visit someone to ask after them'.

en.text: This is my first time here.

am.note: Literally 'coming here, it's my first'.
The job word changes for a woman. Swap in the learner's own job.
ባለትዳር (a married person) is the same for a woman or a man.
Literally 'my years are thirty'.
Literally 'what is your work?'.

en.text: How long have you been here?

am.text: እዚህ ከመጣህ ምን ያህል ጊዜ ሆነ?
am.translit: əzzih kämät'ah mən yahəl gize honä?
am.note: Literally 'since you came here, how much time has it been?'.

addressee_f.text: እዚህ ከመጣሽ ምን ያህል ጊዜ ሆነ?
addressee_f.translit: əzzih kämät'ash mən yahəl gize honä?

addressee_pol.text: እዚህ ከመጡ ምን ያህል ጊዜ ሆነ?
addressee_pol.translit: əzzih kämät'u mən yahəl gize honä?

am.note: Swap in any produce. Add ኪሎው (the kilo) to ask the price per kilo.
Adapted: people just say 'lower it a little for me', not 'can you'. This is the market phrase.
Literally 'let me give you eighty' (birr).
Literally 'the two for a hundred birr?'.

en.text: Do you have a bigger one?

am.note: Literally 'do you have one bigger than this?'.
በቃ = 'that's enough / that's all'.

en.text: Do you have change for two hundred?

am.note: Literally 'do you have change of two hundred?'. Adapted: two hundred, not five hundred. Two hundred is the largest note in everyday use; larger notes were announced in 2024, so re-check before release. In the market scene the change is twenty.
telebirr is Ethiopia's everyday phone money.
Literally 'here it is for you'. Hand things over with the right hand, or both hands to an elder.
Literally 'leave the change'.
Counting drill; these are amounts, not notes.
Literally 'what shall I give you?'. Seller to the learner.

en.text: Okay, how much will you pay?

am.note: Literally 'what else shall I give you?'.
Two kilos at ninety. Amharic says 'hundred eighty' with no 'and'.
መናኸሪያ = the bus terminal for buses between towns.
Agree the bajaj fare before you get in.

en.text: Take me to the market, please.

am.text: ቀጥ ብለህ ሂድ፣ ከዚያ ወደ ግራ ታጠፍ።
am.translit: qät' bəläh hid, käzziya wädä gra tat'äf.

addressee_f.text: ቀጥ ብለሽ ሂጂ፣ ከዚያ ወደ ግራ ታጠፊ።
addressee_f.translit: qät' bəläsh hiji, käzziya wädä gra tat'äfi.

addressee_pol.text: ቀጥ ብለው ይሂዱ፣ ከዚያ ወደ ግራ ይታጠፉ።
addressee_pol.translit: qät' bəläw yəhidu, käzziya wädä gra yəttat'äfu.

am.note: To a bajaj or car driver. In a shared minibus taxi you call out ወራጅ አለ! (wärraj allä!, 'someone is getting off!') instead.

en.text: Is this the way to the hospital?

am.text: ወደ ሆስፒታል የሚወስደው መንገድ ይሄ ነው?
am.translit: wädä hospital yämmiwäsdäw mängäd yəhe näw?

en.text: Which minibus goes to the market?

am.text: ወደ ገበያ የሚሄደው ታክሲ የትኛው ነው?
am.translit: wädä gäbäya yämmihedäw taksi yätəññaw näw?
am.note: Adapted: in Addis the shared ride is the blue-and-white minibus, called ታክሲ (taxi).
Literally 'it is to go to the market'. It mirrors the question ወዴት ልትሄድ ነው? Already on the way, people say ወደ ገበያ እየሄድኩ ነው። Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'the road got lost on me'. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Adapted: drivers just name the amount ('it will be fifty birr'), so it does not change with the listener.
Literally 'reach me!', shouted to everyone.
መድኃኒት ቤት (medicine house) is the other common word.
Literally 'I'm a little sick'. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'my head hurts me'.

en.text: Do you have something for a headache?
Three times a day, after food?

am.note: Literally 'they stole my bag on me': the -ብኝ ending marks the loss as yours. ቦርሳዬ ተሰረቀ (my bag was stolen) is also said.

en.text: Hello, what can I get you?

am.note: Adapted: the service phrase, literally 'what shall I be ordered?'. It is the same for every customer.

en.text: Take two, three times a day.

am.text: በቀን ሦስት ጊዜ ሁለት ሁለት ውሰድ።
am.translit: bäqän sost gize hulätt hulätt wəsäd.
am.note: ሁለት ሁለት = 'two each time'.

addressee_f.text: በቀን ሦስት ጊዜ ሁለት ሁለት ውሰጂ።
addressee_f.translit: bäqän sost gize hulätt hulätt wəsäji.

addressee_pol.text: በቀን ሦስት ጊዜ ሁለት ሁለት ይውሰዱ።
addressee_pol.translit: bäqän sost gize hulätt hulätt yəwsädu.

am.note: Literally 'it tastes very good'.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'may I add a little?', for serving yourself. To ask the host to add more: ትንሽ ጨምርልኝ። (f ትንሽ ጨምሪልኝ።, respect ትንሽ ይጨምሩልኝ።).
On fasting days (most Wednesdays and Fridays) many dishes are meat-free anyway.
Literally 'does it burn?', the everyday way to ask if food is spicy.
Literally 'what all is there today?'.
Literally 'bring me the bill, please'.

en.text: Thank you for the food. Bless your hands.

am.note: 'May your hand be blessed', said to the cook. The female form is the one heard most, since the cook is often a woman.
Literally 'okay, thank you, I'll come'.

en.text: What would you like, tea or coffee?

am.note: Literally 'what shall I treat you to?'. Offering means the host pays.

en.text: Would you like something to eat?

am.note: Literally 'shall I bring you something to eat?'.
ስኒ is the small coffee cup. Literally "drink another cup".
Literally 'come another time too'.
Adapted: neighbours invite you for coffee, not tea ('come later so we drink coffee').
ባለቤቴ (my spouse) is the polite word; ሚስቴ (my wife) is also said. Written style: ይህች. ይቺ is colloquial: in front of elders many people drop it and say ባለቤቴ ናት።
ባለቤቴ (my spouse) is the polite word; ባሌ (my husband) is also said. Many women speak of a husband in the respect form: ባለቤቴ ናቸው።

Literally 'it's to visit you that we came'. Said to an elder, so the base is the respect form. To an older couple at once, use the plural ልንጠይቃችሁ, which is respectful too. The m/f forms are for people your own age.
Base is the respect form to an older man; the variant is to an older woman.

en.text: The journey was good, thank God.
She's well. She sends her greetings.

am.note: Literally 'they are well; they have said peace to you'. Your own mother, spoken of to an elder, takes the respect plural (ናቸው, ብለው-). Among friends people also say ደህና ናት። ሰላም ብላሃለች። (f ብላሻለች).
Literally 'say hello to the family for me'.

en.text: May God give you long life.

am.note: A blessing for an elder, so the base is the respect form. To an older couple at once, use the plural ይስጣችሁ. The m/f variants are for a man or a woman your own age.

en.text: Yes, we have to go. Thank you for everything.

am.text: አዎ፣ መሄድ አለብን። ስለ ሁሉም ነገር እናመሰግናለን።
am.translit: awo, mähed alläbbən. səlä hullum nägär ənnamäsäggənallän.

en.text: Sit down. How was the journey?

am.note: Literally 'is your mother well?'.
Literally 'add a little'.
Hosts often add ምነው ቸኮልክ? (why the hurry?).

en.text: The network is bad. I'll call you back.

am.note: Only 'I'll call you' changes with the listener.
Literally 'my battery is about to run out'.

en.text: I'll be there in ten minutes.

am.note: Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Literally 'do you have time tomorrow?'.

en.text: Let's meet at ten in the morning.

am.note: Ethiopian clock: hours count from dawn (six o'clock European time), so ten in the morning is 'four o'clock in the morning'. If unsure, ask: በኛ ነው በፈረንጅ? (our time or European time?).

en.text: Let's meet at the bus station.

am.note: Literally 'let's meet at the bus station'. ጋ (short for ጋር) marks the place.
Literally 'how much is your phone number?'.

Literally 'I am taken up now'. Also said: አሁን ሥራ ላይ ነኝ (I'm at work now). ሥራ በዝቶብኛል means 'I'm swamped with work', a general state. Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form. Young people in Addis also say ቢዚ ነኝ.
Literally 'okay, I'll come'.

en.text: A little. Can we talk later?

am.note: Literally 'a little. What if we talk later?'.
Only 'you' changes, with the listener. 'I' is the same for a woman or a man. The short ይቅርታ፣ አይሰማኝም። (sorry, it's not coming through) is the same for everyone.
Literally 'let's meet tomorrow'. Amharic: the same words for everyone.
Ethiopian clock: 'four o'clock' is ten in the morning, European time.
Literally 'are you taken up?': asks whether you are free to talk now. ሥራ ላይ ነህ? ('are you working?') is also said.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
Amharic 'I' verbs do not change for a woman or a man, so there is one form.
'Happy' does not change with the speaker in Amharic; 'you' changes with the listener.
Addis Ababa is high and often cool; this fits the lowlands and dry-season afternoons.

en.text: Yes, it's too hot for me.

am.note: Literally 'yes, the heat is too much for me'.
Muslims say አልሐምዱሊላህ (alhamdulillah).
Muslims, and many others, say ኢንሻአላህ (inshallah).
አይዞህ is the everyday word of comfort: 'take heart'.
Literally 'may God heal you', what everyone says to someone who is ill.
Literally 'how did you spend Saturday and Sunday?'.

en.text: Fine, thank God. How was your weekend?

am.text: ደህና ነኝ፣ እግዚአብሔር ይመስገን። ቅዳሜና እሁድ እንዴት አሳለፍክ?
am.translit: dähna näñ, əgziabəher yəmäsgän. qədamena əhud əndet asalläfk?
am.note: 'Fine' does not change with the speaker in Amharic; the question changes with the learner.

addressee_f.text: ደህና ነኝ፣ እግዚአብሔር ይመስገን። ቅዳሜና እሁድ እንዴት አሳለፍሽ?
addressee_f.translit: dähna näñ, əgziabəher yəmäsgän. qədamena əhud əndet asalläfsh?

addressee_pol.text: ደህና ነኝ፣ እግዚአብሔር ይመስገን። ቅዳሜና እሁድ እንዴት አሳለፉ?
addressee_pol.translit: dähna näñ, əgziabəher yəmäsgän. qədamena əhud əndet asalläfu?

am.note: Literally 'will you drink tea?'. At work the offer is often ቡና (coffee) instead.

en.text: Drink the third one, it's the blessing.
Sit down. How was the journey?
She's well. She sends her greetings.
May God give you long life.
Do you have change for two hundred?
Yes, it's too cold for me.
I'm fine, thank you. And you?

blurb.en: The neighbour at the compound gate in the morning: greetings in rounds, family news, and a call for coffee.
An open vegetable stall like the ones at Merkato: prices per kilo in birr, and fair bargaining.
A bajaj where you agree the fare first, or the blue-and-white minibus taxi with its woyala calling the route.
The coffee ceremony at home: beans roasted and brewed in a jebena, incense, popcorn, and three rounds.
The neighbourhood pharmacy: explain a small problem, repeat the dose back, and pay in birr.
Visiting relatives on the weekend: respect forms for elders, food pressed on you, and a blessing as you leave.
Making a plan by phone in Ethiopian clock time, on a line that sometimes drops.
Morning greetings with colleagues, the coffee or tea break, and a meeting set in Ethiopian hours.

meaning.en: Patience and small steps get you there. What is helpless today grows into something that walks.

proverbs.literal: Slowly, slowly, the egg will walk on its own legs.

meaning.en: Weak people who unite can overcome something strong.

proverbs.literal: When spider webs join together, they can tie up a lion.

meaning.en: Work done in a hurry falls apart. Haste makes waste.

proverbs.literal: What you tie on while running comes loose while running.

meaning.en: Stay alert; the careless person gets caught out.

proverbs.literal: The one who did not suspect was pulled out by the roots.

meaning.en: People help themselves to what belongs to the naive person.

proverbs.literal: The plough beam is cut from the fool's doorstep.

meaning.en: Acting brave, or acting at all, once the danger has passed is too late.

proverbs.literal: The dog barked after the hyena had left.

meaning.en: Drink makes people say what they were keeping inside.

proverbs.literal: What the belly hides, malt brings out.

meaning.en: People can be friendly with the very person who means them harm, without knowing it.

proverbs.literal: The ox spends the day with the one who will slaughter it.

meaning.en: You can't miss what you have never had or known.

proverbs.literal: You don't feel homesick for a country you have never known.

meaning.en: Acting too early, before the moment has come.

proverbs.literal: The leaf is broken off before the goat has even arrived.

meaning.en: When someone is down, everyone piles on.

proverbs.literal: A fallen tree gets many axes.
